# How to Adjust Camber on a 1999 Chevy Suburban

You have installed four-inch spindles on your 1999 C1500 frame, but the resulting negative camber is excessive and threatens tire longevity. The immediate issue isn't just that the angle is wrong; it's that the geometry has shifted fundamentally because you've replaced components designed for a specific ride height with parts intended for a lifted stance without updating the rest of the suspension architecture. On a unibody vehicle or even a dedicated lift kit, you might expect adjustable control arms, but the 1999 Suburban utilizes a solid axle rear and independent front suspension that relies on fixed geometry at the factory.

The core problem with attempting to adjust camber on this specific chassis after installing spindles is that the stock upper control arm bushings are not designed for fine-tuning. In many independent suspension setups, including the GM D-body used in late 90s trucks and SUVs, camber gain is a function of the control arm's mounting points relative to the spindle center. When you drop the spindle down with a four-inch lift, the top mount effectively moves outward or downward depending on the specific spindle design, introducing negative camber that the lower arm cannot counteract because it operates in tension only and pivots around a fixed point.

To correct this, you must treat the upper control arm as a variable component rather than a fixed one. The most reliable method involves replacing the stock upper control arms with adjustable units. These arms feature an eccentric bolt or a threaded sleeve that allows you to rotate the mount point on the chassis frame or unibody structure. By rotating the mounting flange, you change the effective length of the arm relative to the spindle axis, thereby altering the camber angle without affecting ride height or caster significantly.

If replacing the entire arm is not feasible due to budget constraints, a simpler but less precise alternative exists: modifying the upper control arm bushing location. This involves drilling out the existing bolt holes in the chassis strut tower and welding new, higher or more outward positioned holes directly to the frame rail. Once welded, you can install a standard bushing into the new hole. However, this approach requires significant fabrication skills and precise measurement. You must ensure that the new pivot point aligns perfectly with the spindle's center of rotation; any deviation here will introduce unwanted toe changes or create binding during suspension travel.

Another option is to use an adjustable camber kit specifically designed for the 1999 Suburban upper A-arms. These kits typically feature a sleeve that slides into the existing arm and allows you to rotate the spindle mount relative to the chassis. Before purchasing, verify that your specific upper control arms are compatible with the adjustment mechanism. Some aftermarket spindles come with their own built-in camber adjustment via an eccentric bolt on the spindle itself, but if you have already installed a non-adjustable four-inch spindle, your only recourse is the control arm.

When executing this modification, pay close attention to the bushing material. Replacing rubber polyurethane or stock rubber bushings with hardened urethane can improve handling response, but it may also increase noise and vibration if not torqued correctly. Always use high-quality grease compatible with your chosen bushing material. Furthermore, after adjusting the camber, you must check the caster angle. On solid rear axles and independent front ends like this one, changing the upper arm geometry often alters caster. If caster drops too low, steering stability will suffer, especially at highway speeds.

Finally, consider the implications for the lower control arm. While the lower arm primarily sets ride height and toe when the spindle is fixed to the strut tower, some aftermarket setups allow for slight camber correction by altering the lower mount position. However, this is rarely sufficient to counteract four inches of lift-induced negative camber. The primary adjustment must happen at the top. If you proceed with welding new holes or installing adjustable arms, perform a wheel alignment afterward. A professional alignment machine is essential here, as visual estimation will not account for the precise degrees required to prevent uneven tire wear. Without proper alignment, even the best adjustable parts will fail to protect your tires.
